name: Lhasa
tagline: The holy city of Tibetan Buddhism
summary: At 3,650 m on the Tibetan plateau, Lhasa is the spiritual heart of Tibetan Buddhism. Pilgrims walk clockwise around the Jokhang Temple and spin prayer wheels below the Potala Palace, the former winter home of the Dalai Lamas, while great monasteries like Sera and Drepung sit on the hills around the city.
seasonNote: April to June and September to October are clear and mild. July and August are the busiest and wettest. Winter is cold but sunny and quiet. Tibet often closes to foreign visitors for weeks around February and March, and around sensitive dates, so check before you book.
arrival: Foreign visitors need a Tibet Travel Permit as well as a Chinese visa, and must travel on a guided tour booked with a licensed agency, which arranges the permit and meets you at the airport or station. Independent travel is not allowed. Fly from Chengdu, Beijing or Kathmandu, or take the train from Xining (about 22 hours). The altitude is 3,650 m: rest on the first day, drink water and avoid alcohol.
gettingAround: Your guide and driver take you between sights; the old town around the Barkhor is walkable.
cashTip: Carry yuan; mobile payments (Alipay, WeChat Pay) are everywhere, and foreign cards work only in bigger hotels.
foodTip: Momos, thukpa noodle soup, tsampa (roasted barley flour), yak meat and salty butter tea in old town teahouses.
buyTip: Prayer flags, thangka paintings, incense, yak-wool shawls and Tibetan jewellery around the Barkhor.
baseArea: Old town near the Barkhor and Jokhang

connections.note: Seasonal flights; a Tibet group visa is issued in Kathmandu for this route.
Some flights stop in Chengdu or Xining.
Usually with a stop; the train via Xining takes about two days.

items.name: Potala Palace
items.summary: The towering white and red palace of the Dalai Lamas, with chapels, golden tombs and a thousand rooms climbing the hill.
items.expect: Tickets are timed and booked by your guide a day ahead; one hour is allowed inside; many stairs at high altitude.
items.tip: Walk the pilgrim circuit (kora) around the base at dawn, then see the palace from Chakpori hill at sunset.
items.why: The symbol of Tibet and a World Heritage Site.
flow: White Palace, then Red Palace chapels.

items.name: Jokhang Temple
items.summary: The holiest temple in Tibet, home to the Jowo Shakyamuni statue, with pilgrims prostrating at its gates.
items.expect: Dim, crowded chapels lit by butter lamps; a rooftop with golden roofs and views of the Potala.
items.tip: Go in the morning when pilgrims fill the halls, and walk clockwise.
items.why: The destination of pilgrims from all over Tibet.
flow: Watch the prostrations at the gate.

items.name: Barkhor Street
items.summary: The pilgrim circuit around the Jokhang, lined with stalls, teahouses and old Tibetan houses.
items.expect: A steady clockwise stream of pilgrims with prayer wheels and beads; security checkpoints at the entrances.
items.tip: Join the flow clockwise and stop at a rooftop café to watch.
items.why: The living heart of old Lhasa.

items.name: Sera Monastery
items.summary: A great Gelug monastery where monks debate in a courtyard, clapping to make their points.
items.expect: The debates usually run in the afternoon on most weekdays.
items.tip: Ask your guide to time the visit for the debate, around 3 pm.
items.why: Monastic life you can watch, not just old halls.

items.name: Drepung Monastery
items.summary: Once the largest monastery in the world, a white town of halls on the mountainside.
items.expect: Steep lanes between chapels.
items.tip: Go in the morning, then walk down to the Nechung oracle temple below.
items.why: The scale of Tibetan monastic life.

items.name: Norbulingka
items.summary: The Dalai Lamas' summer palace in a large park of pavilions and gardens.
items.expect: Quiet gardens; busy during the Shoton yoghurt festival in August.
items.tip: Pair it with Drepung on the same side of town.
items.why: A gentler, greener side of Lhasa.

items.name: Ganden Monastery
items.summary: The mother monastery of the Gelug school, high on a ridge with a pilgrim path around it.
items.expect: About 1.5 hours by road; the kora takes an hour at 4,300 m.
items.tip: Save it for after you have adjusted to the altitude.
items.why: Huge views over the Kyichu valley.

items.name: Yamdrok Lake
items.summary: A turquoise sacred lake below snow peaks, reached over the 4,900 m Kamba La pass.
items.expect: A full day trip, often on the way to Gyantse and Shigatse.
items.tip: Bring warm layers; it is windy at the pass.
items.why: One of Tibet's three holy lakes.

items.name: Momos and thukpa
items.summary: Yak or vegetable dumplings and hand-pulled noodle soup in simple Tibetan restaurants.
items.expect: Cheap, filling and warm.
items.tip: Try yak-meat momos once.
items.why: The everyday comfort food of Tibet.

items.name: Butter tea and tsampa
items.summary: Salty yak-butter tea and roasted barley flour in a crowded pilgrim teahouse.
items.expect: Long benches, thermoses of tea and very low prices.
items.tip: Sweet milk tea is the easier first sip.
items.why: Where Lhasa locals actually sit and talk.
flow: Find a teahouse off the Barkhor.

items.name: Yak and Tibetan set meals
items.summary: Yak stew, sha phaley pies and shapta stir-fry in old-town restaurants with rooftop views.
items.expect: Menus in English near the Barkhor.
items.tip: Try a rooftop restaurant facing the Potala.
items.why: The heartier side of Tibetan food.

name: Lalibela
summary: High in Ethiopia's mountains, Lalibela is a holy town of eleven medieval churches cut down into the rock, linked by trenches and tunnels and still used every day by Orthodox priests and pilgrims. It was built as a New Jerusalem, and at Genna (Ethiopian Christmas) and Timkat thousands of white-robed pilgrims fill it.
seasonNote: October to February is dry and green after the rains. Genna (7 January) and Timkat (19 January) are unforgettable but book out months ahead. June to September is the rainy season.
arrival: Check your government's travel advice before booking: many governments, including Canada, the UK and the US, currently advise against travel to the Amhara region because of armed conflict, and flights and roads can be cut at short notice. When it is open, Ethiopian Airlines flies from Addis Ababa (about one hour), and the airport is 25 minutes from town.
gettingAround: The church groups are a short walk apart in town; hire a licensed local guide at the ticket office.
cashTip: Carry birr in cash; there are few ATMs and cards rarely work. The church ticket is priced in US dollars.
foodTip: Injera with shiro or tibs, honey wine (tej) and the coffee ceremony.
buyTip: Hand-woven cotton scarves, painted icons, carved crosses and Ethiopian coffee.
baseArea: Hotels on the hillside above the churches

connections.note: Via Addis Ababa; check current travel advice for Amhara.
Via Addis Ababa; check current travel advice for Amhara.

items.name: Church of Saint George (Bete Giyorgis)
items.summary: A perfect cross-shaped church carved straight down into the rock, seen from above as you arrive.
items.expect: One ticket covers all the churches for several days; shoes off inside every church.
items.tip: Come in late afternoon when the light turns the rock gold.
items.why: The image of Lalibela and a World Heritage Site.

items.name: Bete Medhane Alem
items.summary: Thought to be the largest monolithic church in the world, ringed by massive carved columns.
items.expect: Covered by the same ticket; priests may show the Lalibela gold cross.
items.tip: Visit early before tour groups.
items.why: The scale of what was carved by hand.

items.name: Bete Maryam
items.summary: Perhaps the oldest of the churches, with painted ceilings and carved crosses.
items.expect: Next to Medhane Alem, linked by a rock passage.
items.tip: Look up at the painted ceiling and the carved stars.
items.why: The most beautiful interior in Lalibela.

items.name: Eastern church group
items.summary: Bete Amanuel, Bete Gabriel-Rufael and others, linked by dark tunnels and narrow trenches.
items.expect: Uneven steps and a pitch-dark tunnel walk (the passage to hell, then light).
items.tip: Bring a small torch and go with a guide.
items.why: The most atmospheric maze of passages.

items.name: Asheton Maryam Monastery
items.summary: A cave monastery high above town, reached by a steep hike or mule ride.
items.expect: About two hours up on foot; a small separate fee.
items.tip: Start early and bring water.
items.why: Views over the whole Lasta mountains.

items.name: Yemrehanna Krestos
items.summary: An older church built inside a cave, of wood and stone layers, about an hour's drive away.
items.expect: A rough road, then a short walk; a separate fee.
items.tip: Combine with the Na'akuto La'ab cave monastery on the way.
items.why: Some think it is finer than the town churches.

items.name: Injera with shiro and tibs
items.summary: Spongy sourdough flatbread with a chickpea stew or fried meat, eaten by hand from a shared plate.
items.expect: Simple local restaurants; Wednesdays and Fridays are fasting days with vegan dishes.
items.tip: Order a beyaynetu platter on fasting days.
items.why: The heart of Ethiopian food.
flow: Tear the injera with your right hand.

items.name: Tej honey wine
items.summary: Golden honey wine poured into a round-bottomed flask in a tej house.
items.expect: Strong and sweet; locals sing and dance in some tej houses.
items.tip: Ask for a smaller flask first.
items.why: A drink you will not find elsewhere.

items.name: Coffee ceremony
items.summary: Beans roasted over charcoal, ground by hand and served in three rounds with incense and popcorn.
items.expect: Takes about an hour; often offered by guesthouses.
items.tip: Stay for all three rounds; leaving early is rude.
items.why: Ethiopia is coffee's birthplace.
